extracted.intended_audience: researchers, graduate students, and advanced readers interested in foundations of mathematics, constructivism/intuitionism, and non-standard analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative, critical analysis of classical vs intuitionistic notions of mathematical meaning, focusing on constructivist standards (Bishop, Brouwer, Heyting, Dummett, etc.) and their relation to non-standard analysis and applications in physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of Excluded Middle (LEM) as dividing criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of excluded middle is the key ingredient in a proof by contradiction and the principal item rejected by intuitionists; rejection of LEM distinguishes intuitionistic logic (InLo) from classical logic (ClLo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that LEM is central to classical proofs (e.g., proofs by contradiction such as the classical proof of irrationality of √2) and that intuitionistic logic rejects LEM, resulting in different acceptable proof techniques and meanings. See (2.1) and Example 2.1 for illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical meaning / constructive content
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical statements and proofs should have numerical or computational meaning: existence claims must provide a construction or a computable witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bishop’s emphasis that 'if you say something exists you ought to be able to produce it' underlies the demand for constructive content. The √2 example contrasts a classical indirect proof with a 'numerically meaningful' constructive proof that exhibits explicit lower bounds separating √2 from rationals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of proofs by contradiction for existence claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Deriving existence from a proof by contradiction (via LEM) is not acceptable constructively unless one can produce a witness or algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Billinge’s account of Bishop’s view and the discussion of classical vs constructive proofs stress that a proof that only rules out non-existence (without producing an instance) is 'flimsy' from a constructivist standpoint. The article gives the √2 example and the meta-argument about consistency as illustrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited Principle of Omniscience (LPO) as non-constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: LPO — 'it is possible to search a sequence of integers to see whether they all vanish' — is characterized as a form of excluded middle and rejected by Bishop and constructivists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors explain LPO, note Feferman's identification of LPO as a special case of LEM, and link standard constructions of hyperreals/Robinson-style infinitesimals to reliance on LPO (hence non-constructivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive quantifiers and restricted domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifiers should range over constructive entities only; intuitionistic (constructive) quantifiers are 'verificational' and differ from classical ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 2.2 contrasts formulas with ClLo-quantifiers versus InLo-quantifiers, showing that replacing ClLo by InLo on all quantifiers yields a constructively acceptable statement that does not imply LEM. The article notes 'inhabited' vs 'non-empty' linguistic precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of Choice (AC) and constructivist scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of (classical) axiom of choice is problematic for constructivists because certain forms of choice imply LEM and produce counterintuitive consequences (e.g., Banach–Tarski).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper presents two approaches to AC (accept infinite sets but accept strange behaviour vs re-examine axioms), references Goodman-Myhill results, and explains that some forms of choice (even finite-choice-like statements over sets of reals) can imply LEM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodman–Myhill theorem as a criterion implicating LEM
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain combinatorial/set-theoretic statements (as framed by Goodman–Myhill) imply the law of excluded middle and thus are non-constructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the axiom-of-choice example (2.2) the authors note that formula (2.2) implies LEM by the Goodman–Myhill theorem (see Section 4.2), illustrating how some plausible-sounding choice principles are constructively unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive definition of irrationality and explicit bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrationality must be defined constructively by giving concrete separation between the real and every rational m/n, expressed in terms of the denominator n (explicit lower bounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 2.1 supplies a constructive approach: exhibit positive lower bounds for |√2 − m/n| in terms of n to provide a constructively adequate proof, in contrast to the classical parity-contradiction argument that uses LEM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive finiteness vs subfinite / (sub)finite distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive treatments distinguish constructively finite (and other constructive notions like subfinite) sets from classical finiteness; these distinctions affect which choice principles and proofs are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article indicates (Section 4.2 and Example 2.2) that certain set classifications (constructively finite vs subfinite) determine whether axioms like the finite axiom of choice are provable and whether they imply LEM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brouwerian counterexamples constrain acceptable domains
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid classical counterexamples (e.g., 'every function is continuous'), Bishop restricts attention (e.g., to uniformly continuous functions) so that intuitionistic/constructive development can proceed without contradiction with classical theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 2.4 explains how Bishop 'finesses' Brouwer's theorems by limiting scope (uniform continuity), and how this is a methodological criterion for what constructive mathematics chooses to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical constructivism vs anti-LEM constructivism (dichotomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct constructive approaches are identified: one focused on 'numerical meaning' (companion view) and another on rejecting LEM as an alternative foundational program (anti-LEM/radical constructivism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subsection 5.1 proposes this dichotomy and frames it as a criterion for evaluating constructivist positions and their amenability to rapprochement with classical mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructivism as companion vs alternative to classical mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A normative distinction: constructive mathematics may be treated either as a companion (coexisting with classical mathematics) or as an alternative (replacement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors use this dichotomy to assess prospects for 'reunifying the antipodes' and to analyze which strands of constructivism might be bridgeable to classical practice (see Section 5 and Table 1.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical meaningfulness ('debasement of meaning')
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedagogical criteria demand that teaching methods preserve mathematical 'meaning' (Bishop's charge that introducing non-standard analysis into calculus courses could be a 'debasement of meaning').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3.1 recounts Bishop's view that calculus taught via Robinson-style infinitesimals might 'debase' meaning, stressing that pedagogical adoption should be judged by how well it preserves computational/numerical clarity and meaning for learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension and transfer principles of non-standard analysis as non-constructive features
rubrics_metrics.description: Robinson-style non-standard analysis relies on extension and transfer principles (and constructions within ZFC + AC) that are seen as non-constructive from an intuitionistic perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3.1 and later analysis note that the transfer/extension axioms and standard model constructions are tied to classical set-theoretic machinery (e.g., ultraproducts, choice) and hence raise constructivist objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to physics as an evaluative test
rubrics_metrics.description: A foundation or constructive framework is judged by whether it can accommodate important physical applications (e.g., variational principles, Hawking–Penrose singularity theorem); currently such applications 'lack a constructive framework'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Abstract and Section 8 emphasize the importance of variational principles and the Hawking–Penrose theorem as challenges: inability to provide constructive accounts for these applications is presented as a vulnerability of constructivism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical narratives: realist vs anti-realist acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical acceptability (realist vs anti-realist narratives) is treated as a criterion shaping how one interprets 'meaning' in mathematics and determines openness to classical devices like hyperreals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors analyze diverging 'insurrectional narratives' (Section 6.3), Dummett, and others, showing that metaphysical stance influences which mathematical constructions are judged meaningful or acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope moderation and arithmetization limits (Kronecker criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kronecker's moderation: only mathematics outside geometry and mathematical physics should be arithmetized; geometry (and irrational numbers) may legitimately fall outside strict arithmetization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 2.1 presents Kronecker's subdivision and his limitation of the constructivist program, offering a criterion for limiting the ambition of constructive reduction to integers based on domain (arithmetics vs geometry/physics).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to phrase quantifier claims linguistically (inhabited vs non-empty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic/formal caution: when switching to intuitionistic quantifiers, replace 'non-empty' by 'inhabited' to avoid excluded-third pitfalls; formulation of statements matters for constructive acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 2.2 and related discussion explicitly mention the customary replacement to avoid linguistic traps, indicating a practical criterion for writing constructively acceptable statements.
